title: Why Adding a Job Made Your Agent Worse (Split It, Don't Grow the Prompt)
description:
You bolted a new job onto your agent, and the jobs it already did got worse. You did not touch the old instructions, so a bigger prompt will not fix this. The fix is to split the agent and put a tiny router in front of the pieces.

Here is the mechanism. Every job you stack lives in the same context window the model reads on every single call. The triage rubric, the review checklist, and a dozen tools now all compete for the same attention budget. So the model spreads thin, and the job you actually cared about gets a thinner slice. This is not a speed problem and it is not a parallelism problem. It is interference inside one context.

Worked example: one agent does retrieval, code review, and ticket triage, all from one giant prompt. Add triage and the reviews slip, because the model is juggling three rulebooks at once. Pull them apart, and a router reads the request, then hands it to the agent built for that one job. Each subagent sees only its own instructions and its own tools, so nothing competes. Three jobs at roughly sixty percent each become three focused agents closer to ninety.

The honest limit: routing only wins when the jobs are independent and share no working memory. The moment two jobs need each other's state, the router just passes data back and forth and you have rebuilt the mess with extra hops.

Every reliable agent I ship looks like this: a thin router over focused parts, not one giant brain holding every job in context. Next time an agent gets worse when you add a skill, do not write a longer prompt. Split the skill into its own subagent and route to it.
